title: Play
summary: Play, also tracked as PlayCrypt and GOLD IONIC, is a ransomware operation that appeared in public reporting from mid-2022 and has since been observed across government, healthcare, manufacturing, professional services and technology organisations in North America, South America and Europe. Its established pattern is double extortion: data is copied out before encryption begins, and the operators publish or threaten to publish it if payment is refused, so recovery from backups alone no longer removes the pressure. Public advisories describe initial access gained through exploitation of internet-facing services, including virtual private network and remote access appliances, followed by credential theft, service creation for persistence, and lateral movement with a mix of legitimate administration utilities and commonly abused attack tooling. A distinctive technical behaviour highlighted by analysts is intermittent or partial encryption, where only portions of files are encrypted to reduce processing time and shorten the window in which defenders can react. The operators have also been reported to delete volume shadow copies and to interfere with recovery options, which raises the cost of restoration. Evidence in a defended environment accumulates in stages: authentication from unusual locations to remote access appliances, new services or scheduled tasks, command shell activity on servers, archive creation and large transfers to file sharing services, and finally mass file modification. The frequent misunderstanding is that endpoint protection alone is sufficient; because the entry point is often a remote service and the payload is deployed through administrative channels, patch management, remote access hardening and identity monitoring carry equal weight. Attribution to a specific country or sponsor is not established in public reporting.

beginner.definition: Play is the name of a criminal group that attacks companies with ransomware. Ransomware is software that locks your files and demands payment to unlock them. This group also copies files first, then threatens to publish them if you refuse to pay. Public reports describe attacks on hospitals, government offices and businesses since 2022.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many companies believe good backups are enough. They are not, because this group steals the data as well. Even with perfect backups, private documents can still appear online. The group also looks for weak remote access. That is the door many organisations leave open for staff working from home. Fixing that door, and watching it closely, is one of the most effective things you can do.
howItWorks: The attackers find an internet facing service with a known weakness, such as a remote access point.
They use it to enter, then steal or guess accounts with more permissions.
They create services and tasks so they can return after a restart.
They move to servers, turn off recovery features, and copy valuable files out.
They start encrypting files, often only parts of each file, to finish faster.
They demand payment and threaten to publish the copied data if refused.
beginner.example: Imagine thieves who enter a warehouse through a side door that was left unlocked. Before they touch the shelves, they photograph every document in the office and send the pictures away. Then they glue the shelving together so nothing can be moved. Even if you have a perfect copy of every box in another building, the photographs are already gone. That is why this kind of attack hurts twice, once from the lockout and once from the leak.
takeaways: Backups are essential but not enough, because data is stolen before files are locked.
Harden and monitor every remote access service, since it is a favourite entry point.
Detect the preparation stage, such as new services and bulk copying, before encryption starts.

objectives: Explain the double extortion model and why backups alone do not neutralise it.
Describe the common entry route through exposed remote access services and how to reduce it.
Identify detection opportunities during the preparation stage before encryption begins.
Explain what intermittent encryption is and why it shortens defender response time.
Describe how recovery features are targeted to raise the cost of restoration.
Recommend preparation steps for an organisation facing a destructive extortion incident.
